crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript covers turning research results into a structured paper, including the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, missing counter-evidence, and overclaimed conclusions in a manuscript before it reaches reviewers.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language refers to the specialized vocabulary, grammatical patterns, and rhetorical conventions that mark writing within a particular academic field, and how these conventions shape peer review.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection in academic writing and peer review covers identifying copied text, paraphrased material, and machine-generated prose in manuscripts, student work, and grant proposals.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a published paper into accessible summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors.

sections.body: This field covers the practical use of artificial intelligence in writing research papers, from first drafts to post-publication explanation. AI systems now generate abstracts, introductions, and literature summaries, and they can reformat citations or suggest clearer phrasing. Researchers also use them to run a draft past a simulated critical reader, checking whether an argument holds together before submission. The site's library of 135 research papers and 11075 extracted claims gives a sense of the scale of material these tools are trained on and tested against. In practice, the work is about assistance, not replacement, a human author still decides what the paper argues and what evidence counts.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands at a point where language generation is fluent but argument checking is shallow. Drafting tools can produce a plausible manuscript section in seconds, yet they do not understand the underlying evidence and will confidently state false or unsupported claims. Plagiarism and AI detection tools exist, but they are not reliable enough to serve as proof of misconduct, and they produce both false positives and false negatives. Disciplinary register models can imitate the style of a field, but they often miss the specific expectations of a particular journal or subfield. The honest limit is that no current system can take responsibility for the truth of a paper, and peer review still depends on human judgment.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Drafting a Manuscript to see how AI can help assemble sections and manage references, then move to Testing Arguments Before Peer Review to learn how a draft can be stress tested before sending it out. Disciplinary Register and Language explains how tools adjust tone and vocabulary for a specific field, while Plagiarism and AI Detection covers the limits of checking originality and spotting machine generated text. Finally, Explaining Research After Publication shows how the same tools can turn a finished paper into plain language summaries or answers for a wider audience. Together these pages move from the first blank page to the moment a paper reaches readers outside the review process.
